speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on this motion, because 1 think it is important. We are talking about a proposal to reduce or abrogate certain powers conferred by the clause in question. The main thrust of the motion was that in the case of a treaty between the Government of Canada and a foreign administration or government, Parliament should be involved in the process of accountability. As we know, Canada is now engaged in trade negotiations, in which major aspects of our sovereignty and our ability to take steps to protect ourselves are at stake, and these negotiations are about to be finalized. I am referring more specifically to the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement on so-called free trade, and we have a number of problems with this.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that agreements between Canada and the United States cover over 80 per cent of our trade in goods and services, providing for duty-free entry. This leaves 20 per cent of our trade that is subject to tariffs and levies, on both sides, to protect the service and manufacturing sectors.
Although this is a relatively small area, Canadians should realize that we must try and retain our control over these tariffs to the greatest possible extent. And I think the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
December 4, 1987
Customs Tariff
Cassidy) would give the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada a chance to take a really close look at such matters. I think it is a very sensible motion.
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 8-and this applies to the various amendments in the group-would amend Bill C-87, an Act respecting the imposition of duties of customs and other charges, to give effect to the International Convention on the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System, and so forth. The proposal is therefore:
That Bill C-87, be amended in Clause 59 by adding, immediately after line
4 at page 19, the following:
"(7) The powers conferred by this section may not be abrogated by any treaty between the Government of Canada and the government of another country except by an Act of Parliament.''
Mr. Speaker, what is being proposed here is that whenever tariffs are imposed by the Canadian Government, an Act of Parliament will be required to implement the measure. For the time being, on the basis of what we know about the free trade agreement-which is not much because the final document is not yet available-the purpose would be to reduce tariffs to a bare minimum.
In other words, the present Government has confronted us with a new situation. The purpose is to eliminate tariff barriers and to open the door to so-called free trade. There are of course a number of exceptions in the proposed agreement, but it is not yet clear what goods are affected, how this agreement is structured and what the powers will be of the mechanism for settling disputes. There are so many documents going around that I think it would be a good idea to have a debate on this question before the agreement is signed, so that we can take a closer look and understand the exact extent of the commitments the Government would have us undertake.
Mr. Speaker, the motion is quite simple. It means that when a Customs tariff is applied or proposed, a Bill would be tabled in the House and Members could consider the question. That is basically what the amendment is about, and I think we will support it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to lead off the debate on the motion originally placed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), who is unable to be here today.
We see this clause as a key one in the legislation. We also see this amendment that we have put forward as crucial to ensure that the Government of Canada is not in a position to implement a trade deal with the United States through the back door. By that I mean that if this House is not in a position to pass the resolution on the deal itself, or in some subsequent enabling legislation, the Government of Canada could use the existing Clause 62 as a means of implementing that trade deal without resorting to approval by Parliament.
Clause 62 allows the Government, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), to reduce or remove customs duties on goods imported from any country without reference to Parliament.
Clause 62(a) indicates that such a reduction has to be by way of compensation for concessions granted by that country or any other country. This clause allows Canada to negotiate at the GATT and to agree to multilateral tariff cuts without having to take them before Parliament, although I am told that the practice has generally been that they do come before Parliament. This clause also allows the Government of Canada to agree to and put into force tariff cuts to the U.S. without reference to Parliament.
We believe that this clause means that it will allow the Government which was stalled in Parliament to implement
December 4, 1987

free trade with the U.S. without bothering to ask for permission.
The amendment that we have before us would restrict the ability of the Minister of Finance and the Governor in Council from going ahead with any tariff reductions with the United States. If this amendment passes, then the Government would be required to come before Parliament to have debated a particular piece of legislation that would implement any reduction in those tariffs between Canada and the United States.
Because this trade agreement, that perhaps is still being negotiated, is so important to Canada and our ability to control our destiny, we feel that it is extremely important that Cabinet, which really is the Governor in Council, not be given the power to implement automatically tariff reductions with the United States. We feel it is of prime importance that the duly elected representatives of the people of Canada, this Parliament and the House, have the opportunity to review publicly and debate publicly the merits of any such tariff reductions. As we have seen, anything that this Government has negotiated has not lived up to the initial image that was created by the Government. It has not ended up being the panacea that we were led to believe. We think Parliament has the responsibility to debate these issues to ensure, whether it is softwood lumber, shakes and shingles, or energy, that the Government be forced to come before Parliament to get permission.
As I stated yesterday, this procedure that we are trying to put in place is very similar to the procedures at the local planning level which establish rules for how a community shall look, and if anyone wants to change those rules, they have to go through a public process. So it is a trigger mechanism, instead of what exists in Clause 62 where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, can say, "We have this deal, and let us implement it", without any of us having the opportunity to go through the ramifications of it, and finding out after the fact what has happened.
In a nutshell, those are basically the concerns that we have. I know that some of my other colleagues wish to make some comments on this Bill, so I will leave it at that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to vote against this motion. The proposed amendment is unacceptable since it is an obvious attempt to discriminate and make representations against the United States. This particular motion is basically the same as Section 11 of the present Customs Tariff. There is no valid reason for including provisions that would discriminate against a specific country and would probably be unacceptable to GATT. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we are here to pass laws that are not only fair but fair to everyone.
Customs Tariff

Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons this motion has been put forward is not perhaps as clearly altruistic as the previous motions we have moved which, as you will recall, attempted to bring more control back to Parliament. This motion does that, but it is also clearly and unabashedly aimed at forcing a debate on issues which we may not, as a House of Commons, get to debate concerning the proposed Canada-U.S. trade deal.
This particular motion, if adopted, would force that deal to come before the House, something that current practice does not do. We do not have a clear opportunity to discuss and debate this deal except by way of opposition motions. Apparently the Government has the intention of putting a motion before the House to discuss the principles of the deal, but we will not be able to debate the proposals clause by clause and see the dotting of the i's and the crossing of the t's. This is just an attempt to demonstrate to the Government that there is another way of going about this.
If we are going to be harmonizing all of our practices with other countries, we should be looking at the practices of some of those other countries to see whether they adopt the practice that we are proposing of sending back national agreements on duty, customs and tariffs as well as larger trade deals to their particular national assemblies, Congress or whatever. If we are going to participate fully and completely in a harmonization process, we think that the process should include harmonization of procedures in the home country, and this amendment would attempt to do that. It would provide the Canadian Parliament with a similar oversight and review provision to what the U.S. Congress has. It would mean that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would have to present these proposals, which do affect revenue and taxation to the House because they are in the legitimate purview of the House and of Parliament. Our amendment would encourage that process being adopted in Canada.
I think I have said it so many times that I do not want to repeat it, but this process is one that was put in train by the McGrath review of the role of the back-bencher, carried on by our friend, the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper), who looked at the methods Parliament uses for controlling the budgetary and taxation process. We have attempted to move amendments throughout the Bill to put some of those ideas into place. This particular amendment goes somewhat toward that as well.
I admit that this amendment is aimed quite directly at the United States with the specific purpose of drawing attention to the fact that we have a very large trade arrangement being proposed between Canada and the United States, an arrangement which the Prime Minister has very modestly referred to as the greatest trade deal in the history of Canada. It is, therefore, likely to have quite an impact on the future history of Canada, so much so that I pointed out to the House

December 4, 1987
Customs Tariff
yesterday-some Members may not have been here at the time-the assessment of Clayton Yeutter who felt that in 20 years Canada would not look at all like it is now because it would be much more integrated with American society.
Members of this House were elected to be given an opportunity to review that kind of revolutionary change. This amendment is one effort to allow it an opportunity for debate on the merits of the initiative. We are proposing that the House have an opportunity to look at such initiatives. Previous amendments we have proposed, if they are adopted, will mean that the House will have, after 60 sitting days, to decide yea or nay whether or not the initiatives are acceptable. It is not a great imposition on any Government. Governments in our system have to operate from the basis of majority. A Government would simply use its majority to push the proposal through, but the House would be carrying on its traditional, long established role of having a full opportunity to review taxing and revenue measures, something which our current practice does not give us.

Motion No. 14
That Bill C-87, be amended in Clause 101 by adding, immediately after line 37 at page 41, the following:
"(4) No remission of duties of a value of more than twenty-five dollars may be made unless it is approved by resolution of both Houses of Parliament."

Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 14 is in the name of my colleague, the Hon.
Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), but moved on his behalf by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).
Basically, Clause 101 allows the Government to remit duties which, at times, is done for routine purposes but can also be done as a back-door way of cutting tariffs if a Government is blocked in Parliament. The purpose of the amendment is, therefore, to allow for routine remission of duties to go forward but to require, when remission is of a value greater than $25 million, that there must be action by Parliament.
We believe that there is a potential loss of revenue for Canada as a result of the trade deal. The value of Canadian tariffs on U.S. imports is about $2 billion a year. The Government insists that consumers will benefit under free trade through lower prices because that $2 billion in tariffs will no longer have to be paid. The question then arises, who will pay it? Will this loss be met by cuts in welfare spending? Will it be met by increased taxes on corporations? Or will it be met by the same average Canadians who were meant to benefit from lower prices?
In line with the principle of parliamentary accountability, we are taking the view that if the Government wants to spend more than $25 million, it should require the approval of Parliament and not by Order implement a major reduction in federal government revenues of which Canadians would be almost unaware.
I think the motion clearly speaks for itself. Once again, we are trying to ensure that the actions the Government takes are taken through the House of Commons and not taken in the cabinet rooms. When decisions are made in the cabinet rooms, we do not have access to the documentation or the justification for the decisions. Here in the House we can sometimes get that kind of information.
At this point I will sit down and allow my colleagues to add their comments should they wish to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think there has been a slight error in the printing of this motion in the Order Paper of December 2. It describes the motion as saying that no remission of duties of a value of more than $25 may be made unless it is approved by resolution of both Houses of Parliament. The intention was that that be $25 million. There is some difference.
With the approval of the House, 1 would ask that the motion be posed as it had originally been intended.

Mr. Speaker, in view of that correction, I am now happy to support the motion. I must say that when I looked at it, I had visions of both Houses being tied up examining items worth $25 each.
The first reason I have for supporting this motion is that under normal circumstances, many powers are given to the Government of the day through Order in Council, but the circumstances now are not normal. This Bill which affects tariffs will itself be affected by the Canada-U.S. trade agreement, the contents of which we still do not know because they are under negotiation at the present time. That being the case, 1 think it is incumbent on us to require that as far as possible, all decisions made under this Bill are brought back to the House for ratification.
There is a further problem with the use of remission orders. While the Financial Administration Act requires that remission orders be published at year end in the Public Accounts of Canada, the costs should also be published. This has not been happening. The Department of Finance has frequently said that for one reason or another, it has been unable to assess the costs accurately and it does not wish to estimate a figure. Therefore, one finds remission orders appearing in the Public Accounts of Canada without any figures attached to them, even though that breaches the Financial Administration Act.
This is something that the Public Accounts Committee has made recommendations on and we are awaiting a government response. We have recommended that rather than publish no figure, the Department of Finance produce its best estimate and clearly identify it as an estimate rather than a firm cost. The problem continues. Members of Parliament are being kept in the dark, both at the time the remission order is made and even up to a year afterwards, since costs are not published in the Public Accounts of Canada. Therefore, I think remission orders should be used as sparingly as possible.
I will therefore support this amendment which provides that any remission order which involves costs of $25 million to the Treasury must be brought before the House and not simply dealt with by Order in Council.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of this amendment because I think it is an important amendment. As we have heard this morning, the Government talked many times about accountability in the House of Commons. Although we are not wed to the figure of $25 million, we think that tariff remissions of a substantive amount should be brought before the House of Commons.
In debating the free trade agreement we have not taken into account that there will be about $2 billion less national revenues collected. When revenues are not collected, they become an expenditure. It is ironic that New Democratic Members are putting themselves in the position of the Conservative Government in that we are quoting that which the Conservative opposition

said so often. The House of Commons should have the ability to decide where a $25 million tariff remission will be taken from. We have heard nothing about how the billions of dollars in revenues which will not be collected will be replaced. In response to questions asked in the House we are told that there will be less spending for consumers as prices will be lower. However, no one talks about how the Canadian Government is going to operate with less revenue. I believe that a government which keeps talking about fiscal responsibility should be accountable. It should be able to tell the House of Commons that when a tariff is remitted, x, y, and z methods will be implemented to replace the revenues. There is nothing in this legislation which says that.
Through this amendment we are asking that any substantive remission be brought before the House of Commons. Our intention is not to obstruct the business of the country. If smaller amounts need to be remitted, we have no problem with that. However, we believe that when it gets to a certain level, the House of Commons should be able to examine it and find out which programs are being cut back or cut out because revenues are not available due to the tariff remission.
I do not think that is too big a step to ask the Government to take. Ordinary Canadians have asked for that kind of accountability for a long time. As I said before, the Government campaigned on that kind of accountability. I do not understand why they object to this now. I believe that it would facilitate the operation of the Government of the day. It would enable Canadians to know exactly what is happening under international agreements. Huge amounts of tariffs would not be remitted without the people of Canada, through the House of Commons, being aware of it.
I, therefore, urge the Members of the House to support this amendment because I believe it will help the operation of the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: PEST CONTROL PRODUCTS ACT-CALL FOR AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Law Reform Commission has released a study entitled "Pesticides in Canada: An Examination of Federal Law and Policy". From it one learns that Canadians are changing their attitude toward the use of chemicals and pesticides.
The study recommends that the Pest Control Products Act be amended to: one, require consideration of groundwater contamination potential when pesticides are proposed for registration; two, provide for public access to health and safety tests relied on in support of a registration application, a 60 or 90-day comment period, and a right to require a hearing before a board review; three, set up a system of priorization for pesticide re-evaluation reviews and to screen registered pesticides to identify those registrations which are based on old or incomplete safety data and for which new evidence suggests they may endanger human health or the environment; four, increase fines under the Pest Control Products Act substantially; five, require that a substantial share of the pest control research budget is spent on research into non-chemical alternatives to pest control.
These are some of the recommendations found in the report entitled "Pesticides in Canada". The Minister of Agriculture
(Mr. Wise) should launch a public review of the Act using this report as a foundation.

subtopic: IMPROVED SERVICE BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND NOVA SCOTIA

speakeroldname: Mr. Pat Binns (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: IMPROVED SERVICE BETWEEN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the level of ferry service between Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Pictou, Nova Scotia, will increase substantially next year. I am pleased to advise the House that the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), has approved 400 additional round trip crossings for the spring and fall months of 1988.
This is great news, not only for the trucking industry but for all people travelling between the Provinces of P.E.I. and Nova Scotia. The people in my riding are particularly pleased because they depend upon this ferry crossing to move goods and services throughout the spring, summer, and fall months.
With a total of some 6,600 round trips expected next year we will see additional employment created at Northumberland Ferries Ltd. and, of course, more goods and services will move between the Provinces of P.E.I. and Nova Scotia.
OO)
That will assist our economy greatly and demonstrates the Government's commitment to upgrade and improve this ferry service. As well, Cabinet is considering the provision of new vessels for the Northumberland ferry service.
I expect that we will soon have a positive decision in that regard. I can tell the House that it is great news for Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: QUINTETTE COAL MINE IN NORTHEASTERN BRITISH COLUMBIA
QUINTETTE COAL MINE IN NORTHEASTERN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia better wake up fast to the reality facing Quintette Coal in northeastern B.C.
The 10 Japanese steel mills that purchase this coal are predictably playing hardball over price. Quintette was originally paid SI02 a tonne and over the past four years has shipped 17 million tonnes, for a total of $1.62 billion, through Prince Rupert. Now the steel mills are paying $95 a tonne and are demanding that the price be lowered to $57.85 a tonne. In
December 4, 1987

fact, southeastern B.C. producers are now receiving only $56 a tonne.
Reports from B.C. indicate that shipments to Japan are now 300,000 tonnes behind schedule, threatening closure of the mine because Quintette has run out of room to stockpile coal.
The difference between the price being paid Quintette and the world price for coal has reached $180 million a year. The Japanese have asked for arbitration to determine whether or not the buyers have the right to terminate the coal purchase contract.
The taxpayers of Canada have put up hundreds of millions of dollars to float this project. Someone in the Government had best wake up to the fact that the Japanese are trying to torpedo it.

Mr. Speaker, earlier this week the Minister responsible for the development of the Montreal region made a statement pertaining to the Picard report which was tabled in this House over a year ago. As if a reminder is necessary, it so happens that this Government has been in office for three years already. Before the election the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had said that he would do everything possible so that Montreal might regain its role as Canada's great metropolitan region. Well, the first move right after the election was to transfer the air transport investigation office from Montreal to Ottawa. First loss of responsibility for the city of Montreal.
Since then the Picard committee was set up and its report included a series of 70 recommendations. The Government took a whole year to act on it, and here is a newspaper article published after the Minister's statement: "Federal commitments in principle were Mr. de Cotret's general response to the recommendations of the Picard report. There was some confusion about which specific aspects of the report had been taken under consideration, so much so that after the Minister's briefing spokesmen for the city of Montreal and the Chamber of Commerce asked for a written summary of commitments made. In a number of cases it is just a matter of continuing studies and consultations about carrying out such or such project. Mr. de Cotret did not make any financial commitment."
This situation is totally unacceptable and, as my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) put it, the Conservative Government took a whole year to produce an utterly meaningless document: nothing but pious wishes, nothing concrete for Montreal East, nothing specific to create jobs in the city of Montreal.

subtopic: ASSOCIATION'S SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT AND TAX REFORM
ASSOCIATION'S SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT AND TAX REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to learn during a recent briefing by the Canadian Mining Association that the Canadian mining industry has been operating financially in the black for the last two quarters and that global metal consumption is at near record highs. This follows six years of depressed global metal prices.
More important, I want to report to the House that the Mining Association of Canada completely supports the enhanced trading relationship with the United States. The background of this is that this industry vital to Canada was facing major import restrictions on potash, uranium and steel products, together with trade barriers being threatened for the base metal industry. The health of these industries is vitally dependent on trade relationships across the North American markets.
Furthermore, the Mining Association supports the White Paper on Tax Reform and, in fact, urges the federal Government to move as quickly as possible to Phase II of tax reform at an early date.
It is reassuring to know that the Canadian mining industry, which is so important to Canada, is returning to economic viability and supports the economic policies of the Government.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT ON PLUTONIUM AIR SHIPMENTS-HAZARD TO CANADIAN NORTH
UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT ON PLUTONIUM AIR SHIPMENTS-HAZARD TO CANADIAN NORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United States and Japan signed an agreement on November 4, 1987, which proposes to have plutonium flown over Canada. The Government has consistently said not to worry about this cancer causing substance being flown over our North because the transport route has yet to be selected.
Yet in a letter dated April 30, 1987, Secretary of State George Schultz said: "On the question of routing, it requires only that the aircraft returning plutonium from Europe to Japan must take a polar route or another route that avoids civil disorder and natural disasters." Given this information, the only possible route is across our North.
I will put money on it that if attempts were made to fly the plutonium powder across the 48 lower States, civil disorder would definitely be provoked.
The Government also said that it would be premature to take action to block these flights because no official request to

December 4, 1987
permit such overflights has been received. If anyone cares to read the agreement, they will see that it is contingent upon air transport of plutonium. In other words, the agreement specifically requires air transport.
Another very important concern is that the Government keeps saying it will only agree to the shipments if safe casks are to be used.
What is the Government's definition of safe? Currently, Canada officially adheres to the International Civil Aviation Organization guidelines. For the air transport of radioactive material, ICAO in turn defers to the International Atomic Energy Agency guidelines which require a cask capable of withstanding a 50 kilometres per hour impact test. We are concerned with air transport, not automobile transport. The Government must say no to plutonium overflights now.

Mr. Speaker, this morning Statistics Canada released the new unemployment figures in Canada. Unemployment is down to 8,2 per cent, the lowest level in six years.
Mr. Speaker, this clearly shows that the efforts made by our Government have brought concrete results, even if Opposition Parties have constantly and fiercely attacked our policies; they are using exactly the same approach with the Free Trade Agreement with the United States.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the months and years to come will do justice to this Government and its great Prime Minister. Deals such as the Meech Lake Accord and the Free Trade Agreement with the United States are historic and extremely profitable for Canadian men and women in general.

subtopic: LOCATION OF PROPOSED SPACE AGENCY-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: LOCATION OF PROPOSED SPACE AGENCY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Last Fall, Mr. Speaker, the Government announced substantial cuts in the budget of the National Research Council as well as major capital expenditures in a new space agency in Canada. In an atmosphere of total confusion which we are getting accustomed to after three years, the Government announced that the space agency would become a major research instrument. At the same time, it was announced that Canada would not
participate in the greatest space research program, namely, the United States' Strategic Defense Initiative.
Since then, nothing! We do not know when or where the new space agency will be established; the promised research resources have not materialized; in short, utter "Mulronian" uncertainty and confusion prevail.
Will the new agency be based in Ottawa? Will it be based in Montreal? Will it be based partly in Ottawa and partly in Montreal? Nobody knows! As a matter of fact, the Minister himself has recognized to the media that the Prime Minister is the only one who knows. He has informed us that he has detailed information, and that it would be a political decision on the part of the Prime Minister.
What really concerns me, Mr. Speaker, is the admission by the Minister responsible for Science and Technology that this will be essentially a political decision of the Prime Minister. We do not need a political decision, but a decision based on good sense applying effectiveness and productivity criteria.
Unfortunately, since coming to power, this Government has not come up with many rational decisions. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this space agency should be established in the National Capital region.

subtopic: NATIONAL STRATEGY WELCOMED-TAX DEDUCTIONS AND CREDITS
NATIONAL STRATEGY WELCOMED-TAX DEDUCTIONS AND CREDITS
speechtext:
Yesterday, I, like millions of Canadian parents, was delighted by the announcement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) with respect to a new national strategy on child care.
The $5.4 billion program over the next seven years will not only double the number of child care spaces in Canada, but will provide a much more realistic tax break for families with young children. Increasing the tax deduction to $4,000 per child for receipted child care expenses for children six years of age and under, will really be a boon to millions of middle-income families across Canada. The $200 a year refundable tax credit recognizes the role of parents who stay at home with their children or use informal baby sitting arrangements.
Most important, this new policy reinforces the rights of parents and provinces to choose the child care arrangement most suitable to their needs. The 75 per cent assistance for non-profit day care centres will certainly expand their activities and their spaces. The new arrangements with the provinces for cost sharing will help the provinces shape programs most suitable to the regions.
December 4, 1987

For the first time after years and years of discussion and debate, it is this Government that has taken real action on child care needs. As a woman, I know that this will ensure that women across the country finally have a chance to reach the goal of economic equality. As a parent, I know that parents as well will now, for the first time, have realistic choices and opportunities to meet their child care needs.

maintopic: WORLD CUP SKI JUMPING COMPETITION AT THUNDER BAY
WORLD CUP SKI JUMPING COMPETITION AT THUNDER BAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the eyes of Canada and the world will be on Thunder Bay this weekend. Big Thunder, the home of the National Sports Training Centre, will be host to 93 competitors, representing 17 countries, at the Molson World Cup of Ski Jumping, the kick off event for this year's international ski jumping circuit.
Canadians will be watching our own team, Horst Bulau, Colin Capel, Tod Gillman, Ian McGrath, Ron Rautio and Ron Richards as they take on the world. We will also be watching young Steve Collins, our Ojibway jumper, as he returns to the World Cup circuit. We all want to wish them good luck.
Thanks go as well to the hundreds of volunteers and the staff of Big Thunder for making this event possible. But the Government of Canada can make it even better. It can announce before this weekend that it has agreed to support Thunder Bay's bid for the 1991 or 1993 World Nordic Games. That would be the cap on an excellent weekend ahead.
I encourage all Canadians to tune into the World Cup this weekend to watch Thunder Bay host the world.

Mr. Speaker, the accomplishments of the Conservative Government of Canada are legion. The record shines with promises fulfilled and an ever improving national economy.
Unemployment, which had continuously increased under the Liberals, in line with their high interest rate policies and constraints on Canadian enterprise, is now being brought under control. Under our new enlightened Government, Canada has seen the creation of over one million new jobs. Today the unemployment rate stands at only 8.2 per cent, the lowest since 1981. In many regions of the country it is virtually zero, and even in hard-core areas people are finding more jobs are available.
The success of Conservative economic policy is evident to the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who were thrown out of work by the Liberal-Socialist coalition but who are now gainfully employed and making good money under the Conservative Government.

Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a telephone call from a woman whose father is in intensive care in the Montreal General Hospital. Much to my surprise, I also received a press release from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) which shows that his Government hid the information about the tainted mussels for at least two days before releasing that information to the public.
It is possible that not only did the Government try to hide the information for two days, but we have information that the mussel tainting may have been hidden for up to seven days, a situation which has put the industry at risk and, more importantly, has put Canadians at risk. This particular woman's father ate those mussels during the period when the Government, in making a public announcement about the situation, could have prevented more Canadians from being hospitalized.
1 call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who issued a statement which clearly showed that for at least two days he did not make a public announcement when he knew about the tainted mussels, to come clean with the public and, in particular, to report to this House why he did not tell Canadians that eating mussels could possibly put them at risk.

subtopic: CHARTERED BANKS-HIGH INTEREST RATES AND CHARGES
CHARTERED BANKS-HIGH INTEREST RATES AND CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the high interest rate charged by Canadian banks is a serious contributor to the cause of our national debt, our farm and small business debt crisis, and the slow growth in our national economy. Not only do chartered banks pay very little income tax but their high interest rates are the reason many selfemployed people do not have to pay income tax themselves.
Banks are also ripping off the public by charges to an account, from taking money out of one's own account to depositing money into one's own account, plus many, many more charges. I was glad to hear the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) say that those charges are going to be investigated.

December 4, 1987
Oral Questions
There is now a 6 per cent spread between some interest paid to customers and interest charged to a borrower.
Banks must be made responsible to the public and must share some fiscal payment to reduce the deficit of the federal Government. Banks should not be looked on as loan sharks but rather as respectable businesses in our society. This can only be attained if they change their ways.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is extremely unfair to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) using his own words but I will do so anyway. On September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister sent a letter to Members of Parliament in which he said about conflict of interests:
We have taken great pains to ensure that the new Code leaves no doubt that the ultimate responsibility for the ethical standards of the federal Government rests with the Cabinet and, more particularly, with me.
He said further:
In carrying out that responsibility the Government is directly accountable to Parliament and through Parliament to the people of Canada. You will find no quasi independent agencies in this Code that will allow the Government to shirk its responsibility by saying that the problem belongs to someone else. Nor will you find anything which will relieve me and my colleagues of the necessity of exercising judgment.
Very clearly, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has failed to exercise judgment when he has maintained in the past that there was no conflict of interest in relation to the issue involving the Member of Parliament for York Peel (Mr. Stevens). Very clearly the Prime Minister has misled the people of Canada-inadvertently probably, of course.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member just saved himself, I guess, by saying it was inadvertent misleading. But whether that "inadvertent" came out as the Speaker rose, I will never know.
Oh, oh!

subtopic: NATIONAL STRATEGY-INCREASED TAX CREDITS AND EXEMPTIONS
NATIONAL STRATEGY-INCREASED TAX CREDITS AND EXEMPTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in this House the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) tabled the federal response to the report of the Special Committee on Child Care, of which I was a member. I would like to compliment the Minister on his announcement. The strategy acknowledges that Canadian
parents should have the choice of child care for their own children. Tax assistance initiatives will respect their choice.
Many low and middle-income families who care for their children at home, or who have a friend or relative care for their children, will be eligible for a new supplement to the refundable child tax credit. This will be increased by $200 a year for a child six years and under. This increase will be phased in over the 1988 and 1989 tax years.
The existing deduction for receipted child care expenses will increase to $4,000 for a child aged six and under, or a child with special needs.
This strategy in no way usurps the provinces' authority but is done in concert and to augment the provincial Governments' child care policies. The National Strategy on Child Care recognizes that parental choice is paramount by offering to families a policy which will help all Canadians.

subsubtopic: PARKER COMMISSION REPORT-CONFLICT OF INTEREST CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On April 30, 1986, I asked the then Deputy Prime Minister about the conduct of the Hon. Member for York-Peel. The Deputy Prime Minister in that Question Period made the following statement:
-the responsibility of the Prime Minister to the House and to the country is to ensure that there has been full compliance with the code of conduct which has been established for the guidance of Ministers of the Crown. That responsibility has been discharged. The Prime Minister, the Government, and 1 are satisfied that there has been full compliance with the code of conduct by the Minister.
That was in April, 1986. I think it is important, on the day following the close of a sorry episode in the life of this Government, the expenditure of over $3 million, the disgrace of a Minister, that we find out here what the Government and the Prime Minister have learned from it all. Does the Prime Minister acknowledge his own responsibility, that his assurance to the House was false that the Hon. Member for York- Peel had done nothing wrong-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PARKER COMMISSION REPORT-CONFLICT OF INTEREST CODE
speechtext:
The House will understand the difficulty that the Chair can be in with respect to this particular subject.
Hon. Members have every right, of course, to ask questions concerning the general issue. However, I wish to make it very clear that the Chair will not allow questions or preambles to amount to a charge of any type against any Member in this place.
December 4, 1987

If it is the desire, or if there is some reason why any charge should be made against anybody, whether they are members of the Cabinet or outside the Cabinet, then there is a proper way to lay that charge, and it is not in Question Period by way of a preamble.
The Hon. Member for York Centre is a very experienced parliamentarian who has occupied positions of high importance and trust in the country, and he knows the rules as well as the rest of us do.
I am not stopping him from asking questions about conflict of interest guidelines, or what the Government may or may not have known at the time, but I will not permit Hon. Members to use preambles to make charges against people. If that is what they feel they must do, there is another way to do it.
The Hon. Member will continue his question and keep in mind the Chair's admonishment.

subsubtopic: PARKER COMMISSION REPORT-CONFLICT OF INTEREST CODE
speechtext:
I will do so, Mr. Speaker.
Does the Prime Minister acknowledge that the guidelines that I referred to, and that he has introduced, were not respected, that the guidelines were not policed at all, and that the Prime Minister had no basis whatsoever for claiming that that Member would be back in Cabinet?

subsubtopic: PARKER COMMISSION REPORT-CONFLICT OF INTEREST CODE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PARKER COMMISSION REPORT-CONFLICT OF INTEREST CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the assurance that I and the Deputy Prime Minister gave to the House was complete and forthcoming, was based on all of the information that we had at that time, and was secured in a proper and appropriate way. That information was shared with the House.
Clearly, when the article first came out, there were meetings between the Deputy Prime Minister and the Assistant Deputy Registrar General, there were meetings between the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister, and there were meetings between myself and the Minister in respect of each and every one of those allegations.
Based on the assurances that we received, the Deputy Prime Minister and I spoke to the House in the manner in which we did. I take back not a word of what I said, because that was based upon information imparted to me and to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Clearly, the Parker Royal Commission, having interrogated and examined this matter very carefully for some 18 months, has adduced new evidence which is before the country. I acknowledge that we accept that version, and will be acting upon it.

The Prime Minister says that he takes nothing back; the Member for York-Peel says that he takes nothing back and did nothing wrong. I began by asking what had been learned from this experience.
Oral Questions
I wish to ask the Prime Minister, in light of all that has happened, has he changed? Are the guidelines going to be enforced? For example, in light of everything that has happened has the Prime Minister taken any steps to assure that those guidelines are now being respected by his Ministers?

Mr. Speaker, I want to be very clear, and I know that my hon. friend would want this not to be subject to any misinterpretation.
When I stated that I take nothing back with regard to what I said, that dealt with the information that I supplied to the House pursuant to an examination of the material and discussions and questions submitted to the Minister by me, by the ADRG, by the Deputy Prime Minister, and conveyed to the House that same day. It is in regard to that that I ask my hon. friend to understand my use of the phrase.
In regard to the conflict of interest guidelines and problems, I appointed an impartial Royal Commission, and a Chief Justice of impeccable character to conduct this investigation fully, which he did. As evidence unfolded before the commission, which only came out in the course of using the instruments available to a Royal Commission and not available to an ordinary Member of the House or even to the Prime Minister, in light of this I instructed the Associate Secretary of the Cabinet, Mr. J. L. Manion, to review personally with each Minister his or her situation under the code very carefully, and advise me in regard to that interrogation.
I received the advice from the Associate Secretary of the Cabinet that, in his opinion, all the principles and the procedures were being complied with in all cases of members of the Cabinet. I share that information with my hon. friend.

subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TELEPHONE CALL TO FORMER MINISTER
PRIME MINISTER'S TELEPHONE CALL TO FORMER MINISTER
speechtext:
The Prime Minister was reported by the Member for York-Peel yesterday as having made what was characterized as a "call of encouragement". In the light of the revelations today, it is interesting that the Prime Minister had discussions or exchanges with the Hon. Member for York-Peel, and in spite of that he was prepared to give him a call of encouragement.
In light of the press release and statement put out yesterday, what was the tenor of that encouragement? Given that the Member for York-Peel does not accept the judgment, he indicates that he is considering appeal, I want to ask whether the encouragement of the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TELEPHONE CALL TO FORMER MINISTER
speechtext:
The difficulty here is strictly procedural, and that is whether or not that question pertains to the administration of the Government. I do not want in any way not to give the Hon. Member the appropriate opportunity to ask questions, but I have some considerable doubt as to whether the private conversation between the Prime Minister and the Member of Parliament relates to the administration of the Government.

December 4, 1987
Oral Questions
I am wondering if the Hon. Member for York Centre might find another way to place his question.

subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TELEPHONE CALL TO FORMER MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me come directly to the public policy aspect. Does the Prime Minister's encouragement include an intention that the taxpayers of Canada should pay for any legal actions now that the Member for York-Peel might take?

subtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TELEPHONE CALL TO FORMER MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the telephone call to which my hon. friend refers took place after the tabling of the report in the House of Commons.
It was a call on behalf of my wife and myself to another human being, to express the sadness that any Member of Parliament would feel at the plight in which he found himself.
It in no way detracted from the statement that I issued wherein we accepted fully the recommendations and the judgments issued yesterday by Chief Justice Parker.
As a human being I would feel the same sadness for any Member of the House irrespective of the Party that he represented.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister on the same topic.
On September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister appointed no less a person than himself to ensure that Ministers complied with the conflict of interest guidelines. Judge Parker concludes in his report that the Minister broke the rules no less than 14 times in his tenure as Minister of the Crown and demonstrated what has been referred to as complete disregard for the rule of conflict of interest.
Will the Prime Minister now admit that he has failed in the discharge of his duty of administering the conflict of interest guidelines in the way he said he would himself? What will he do to ensure that he and his Cabinet colleagues follow the rules now and from here on in?

Mr. Speaker, on September 9, 1985, I took the guidelines that had been set out by Mr. Trudeau, we typed them up, improved upon them, we believed, and conveyed them to all Members of the House. Clearly as I have acknowledged, and as anyone would know, the guidelines are not perfect. They were good in type but clearly imperfect and the judge has referred to that in his Royal Commission Report and we accept that judgment.
I draw the Member's attention to an important statement by the judge at page 361 of his report where he says this:
It is important to remember that no conflict of interest system can, by itself, guarantee ethics in government or prevent dishonourable conduct on the part of cabinet ministers or other public office holders. Ultimately, public trust and
confidence in the integrity of government depends upon the integrity of
individual public office holders and their individual sense of honour.
That is the responsibility upon all of us. While we can and shall act further to improve the Code of Conduct and tighten up even further, as the judge suggests; in respect to conflict of interest, ultimately in the end it is our responsibility as individuals to the House of Commons and to the country.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the last comment of the Prime Minister. Improving guidelines is one thing but changing the attitude of Governments and members of a Government is another.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And of the House.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, considering the fact that the Prime Minister has failed in his task to administer the conflict of interest guidelines, as pointed out by Judge Parker, is the Prime Minister prepared to ask a more competent person to administer these guidelines? Is he prepared to legislate these guidelines and is he also prepared to include penalties, since obviously a code of ethics was not sufficient as far as this Government was concerned?

Mr. Speaker, there is no question of anyone failing in his task to administer conflict of interest guidelines or the like. As Judge Parker pointed out in his sizeable report, it is ultimately the Member's responsibility to behave in accordance with the guidelines at all times. The most fool-proof system in the world is useless unless the Member decides to abide by it. There is the basic issue of human nature. As far as we are concerned, we have carefully read the judge's recommendations, and we will make further improvements and provide even stricter criteria for the guidelines that will be submitted very shortly.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. On the morning of April 29, 1986, knowledge of Mrs. Stevens' loan from someone dealing directly with her husband's Department became publicly available. From that moment on, in the words of Judge Parker, surely there was what he described in the following words:
The mingling of private and public business-that clearly involves a conflict
of interest and is wrong by any measure.
Is the Prime Minister saying today that he still believes he was carrying out his responsibilities at that time in not asking then, promptly and immediately, for the resignation of the Member for York-Peel?

Mr. Speaker, the Member asks me whether I was carrying out my responsibilities. This is the article that appeared that morning
December 4, 1987

in The Globe and Mail, the morning of the twenty-ninth. When it appeared-and this is on the record-I immediately instructed the Deputy Prime Minister to meet with the Assistant Deputy Registrar General to examine this matter. I instructed the Deputy Prime Minister to meet with the then Minister. I met with the then Minister myself. I fully reported to the House in that regard.
On the basis of information and responses provided to us, the decisions we took at the time were appropriate. Clearly in the light and with the benefit of an 18 month royal commission, the evidence adduced during the life of that commission is different from the information imparted to us and of which we had knowledge that morning.
The article appeared when we arrived at the office and at two o'clock we were providing this House with the information that we did. The information that we provided the House with was all of the information that I think any reasonable person could have been expected to acquire in those time frames and with the instruments available to us.
Obviously there has been a change in the perception of a conflict of interest. I do not disagree with the assessment of the judge, given the benefit of his power of inquiry and the opportunity that he had to reflect upon this evidence, to bring down a value judgment in the course of an 18-month inquiry. But I am satisfied that I acted promptly and properly in advising the House as I did at that time.

subtopic: MINGLING OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BUSINESS-TIMING OF REPORT
MINGLING OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BUSINESS-TIMING OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deeply regret the Prime Minister's answer. I am not referring to information that Judge Parker brought out in the course of his inquiry. 1 am not referring to any facts that came out after the twenty-ninth. I am talking about facts that became publicly available, particularly in this instance, that Mrs. Stevens had stated she had made this loan with someone with direct business dealings with her husband's Department. The Minister then admitted that he was aware of that loan on that day.
Given Judge Parker's very concise and, I think, accurate description of what a conflict of interest consists of and his talking about a co-mingling of private and public concerns, surely at that moment when it became public knowledge that that loan had been made to the wife of the Minister, the Prime Minister ought to have understood in the most basic sense that a conflict of interest existed from then on, and he ought to have demanded the resignation of the Minister. Why did he not demand that resignation then?

subtopic: MINGLING OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BUSINESS-TIMING OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should not get exercised. The question deserves an appropriate response. He asks why. The answer is that the public official charged with ensuring compliance of the conflict of interest guidelines, the ADRG, provided the Deputy Prime Minister that very morning with
Oral Questions
the assurance that the Minister in question was in full compliance with the guidelines.
Subsequent to that, in regard to other allegations in the story, there was a meeting between the Deputy Prime Minister and others and the then Minister for a careful examination, as there was with me, prior to coming to the House. 1 conveyed to the House all of the information imparted to me and to my colleagues, and the view of the ADRG.
I acknowledge, with the benefit of this Royal Commission's 18-months work, I can tell my hon. friend without reluctance that if I had had this kind of information available to me, or any semblance thereof, clearly I could have come to a different conclusion. On the basis of the evidence provided to us that day when I spoke to the House, prior to my departure the next day for the Far East, 1 gave my hon. friend and colleagues in the House all of the information that was made available to us, together with the value judgment expressed by the ADRG that the then Minister was in full compliance with the conflict of interest guidelines.

Mr. Speaker, for whatever reason the Prime Minister is simply missing the point. I am talking not about what Judge Parker revealed. Judge Parker was well aware that he had no mandate to pass judgment on the Prime Minister in terms of his exercising his responsibility. Some of us wanted that included in the terms of reference, and the Prime Minister knows it was not included, but 1 want to give the Prime Minister Judge Parker's comments and ask him now if he thinks it was pertinent to the public knowledge that he had at the time? Judge Parker says:
The mingling of private and public business .. . that clearly involves a
conflict of interest and is wrong by any measure.
Since the Prime Minister knew on the morning of April 29, 1986, that Mrs. Stevens had in fact obtained this interest-free loan from a person doing direct business with her husband's Department, does the Prime Minister not agree that Judge Parker's precise description of a conflict of interest applied then and there to the Member for York-Peel? If the Prime Minister does agree with that, why did he not demand his resignation then?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that I knew something, presuming that I knew for certain that that was the truth. 1 did not know. What I did know was that there was an allegation made in a newspaper, and in political life there are many of these. It is incumbent that while we act thoroughly, we act with prudence, and that people at least be given the benefit of some degree of the presumption of innocence.
The newspaper allegation appeared the first thing in the morning. 1 immediately instructed the Deputy Prime Minister to meet with the ADRG who is responsible for ensuring

December 4, 1987
Oral Questions
compliance with the conflict of interest guidelines and received the assurance that there was full compliance. I went further and instructed the Deputy Prime Minister to meet specifically with the then Minister and received further assurances. I met with him myself and received the assurances that I conveyed to Members of the House of Commons.
My hon. friend says in his prefatory remarks that he wanted a certain question included in the terms of reference. I beg to differ with my hon. friend. My recollection is that opposition Parties did not want an impartial Royal Commission at all; they wanted some kind of a parliamentary group. We are the ones who established an impartial Royal Commission to get all the truth out because we had absolutely nothing to hide and we wanted Canadians to have all the truth via an impartial Royal Commission.

subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR ETHICAL STANDARDS OF GOVERNMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR ETHICAL STANDARDS OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Canadians want honesty and morality to be the practice of the Government of Canada. Morality can begin to be restored if Mr. Justice Parker's recommendations on conflict of interest are followed. I believe that honesty can begin to be restored if the Prime Minister accepts today his personal responsibility for the failure of the conflict of interest guidelines authored by the Prime Minister.
In that regard I would ask the Prime Minister if he stands by his words of September 9, 1985, in a letter to all Members of Parliament, in which he said that the ultimate responsibility for the ethical standards of the federal Government rested with the Cabinet and more particularly with him.
If the Prime Minister stands by those words, is he prepared to acknowledge today in light of the findings of the Parker Commission Report that in fact the Prime Minister did not take all the action necessary to enforce his conflict of interest guidelines?

subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR ETHICAL STANDARDS OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is do I accept responsibility for what happens to members of my Government and the answer is yes. That is the responsibility of the Leader, the Prime Minister, and I say that without any hesitation.
If my hon. friend wants to be fair in a sensitive matter that applies to all Members of the House, I would refer him to what the Chief Justice said. He said:
It is important to remember that no conflict of interest system can, by itself, guarantee ethics in government or prevent dishonourable conduct on the part of cabinet ministers or other public office holders. Ultimately, public trust and confidence in the integrity of government depends upon the integrity of individual public office holders and their individual sense of honour.
Having said that, I will say that I think we had what many people would consider to be a good set of conflict of interest guidelines. The judge thinks that they are less than adequate and he has made some recommendations for full disclosure
and other matters that I have accepted, and we will be acting upon them quickly.
I think, in the circumstances, the appropriateness of appointing an independent royal commission to examine fully the conduct of the Minister represented a substantial departure from past practice in regard to allegations made in this House. I think it was helpful to the political process in Canada and provided the beneficial rule changes that have been suggested which the Government will be dealing with very quickly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister for his answer but I believe, with respect, that he missed the point. There have been many occasions when the Prime Minister rose in the House with respect to allegations that had been made, either outside the House or inside the House, and gave the House his personal assurance upon his personal investigation that there had been no problem, no conflict of interest or no wrongdoing.
The Prime Minister is telling us today that in the case of the Member for York-Peel he was wrong in retrospect. That calls into question the process that was followed on the many other occasions the Prime Minister had given similar assurances in the House.
My question is simple. The process of restoring the public's confidence in the morality and honesty of Parliament and the Government of Canada can only begin if the Prime Minister rises in his place today and accepts his personal responsibility for failing to impose a set of conflict of interest guidelines authored by the Prime Minister himself because adequate measures were not taken to investigate and ensure those guidelines were being followed. Will the Prime Minister admit that today?

Mr. Speaker, as I have already indicated, I accept at all times the responsibility for what happens to my Government and my Party and their members. That is a fact of political leadership. One ought never to shirk that responsibility and I am not seeking to, under any circumstances.
My hon. friend is asking whether the conflict of interest guidelines were appropriate. I believed they were when I brought them in. I think many Members on both sides of the House thought they were demanding and exacting when compared with those of other jurisdictions, but clearly that is not a view that is shared by Chief Justice Parker who, having examined this matter, recommends full disclosure and the enactment of legislation in regard to conflict of interest.
Conflict of interest is an extremely complex and difficult human problem. As the judge has pointed out, and I am not trying to hide behind anything the judge has said, the best system in the world will never function unless all Members of Parliament want to live by the spirit and the letter of that law.
December 4, 1987

The best system in the world cannot exist unless human beings agree to be bound by it and to honour it at ail times.
I thought we had made major improvements in past conflict of interest guidelines. I think there is general agreement that we had. Clearly the judge feels that we can improve further on them. In light of the comprehensive review he has made and the seriousness of his recommendations, and indeed the requirement for greater disclosure, I have commended the judge for the thoroughness of his inquiry and the seriousness of his recommendations, and I have indicated publicly the intention of the Government to act quickly in regard to them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. During today's Question Period the Prime Minister is making it appear that if he had the report of the Parker inquiry on April 29, things might have been different. I think Members of the House view the situation somewhat differently.
This is not just a matter of available information. What we do know is that the Member for York-Peel admitted to the knowledge of the interest-free loan on April 29 and Judge Parker has said that from April 29 on there was a conflict of interest by any measure, not just by the measure of the guidelines that were in effect then.
Was it only political pressure that brought the Prime Minister to take action, because the action was not taken on the basis of information alone?

Mr. Speaker, the action I took was the appointment of the independent Royal Commission with full and complete access, something which is most unusual pursuant to actions in this House of Commons.
The reason I took this action was because I felt it was right and appropriate and in the interests of Canada and the Public Service of Canada and those of us who seek to serve the public that this be done. I appointed a royal commissioner and we gave him complete freedom to select as counsel whomever he wished, and to conduct his inquiry in the manner in which he wanted to, and he did a professional job. He brought in a major series of recommendations for improvements. That is why it was done, because it was in the national interest that it be done, and that is what motivated it.
Mr. Speaker, I think many of us in Canada felt, as we listened to the Hon. Member for York- Peel yesterday, that we were having a replay of Richard Nixon.
Oh, oh!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Motion No. 15
That Bill C-87, be amended in Clause 39 by adding, immediately after line 6 at page 54, the following:
(3) Where a tariff and Schedule I is charged as a consequence of an order or regulation made under this section, no additional amount of tariff shall be levied on any good which is imported between the date of coming into force of this act and the date of the order or regulation made under this section.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Motion No. 15 is to eliminate the retroactivity component in the Bill.
Because the harmonized system has been developed over a number of years and is complex by its nature and may well have some adverse and unforeseen effects on certain industries, the Government is giving itself the power, through Clause 139, to change the new tariffs in Schedules I and II for a period of 18 months on a retroactive basis until January 1, 1989.
Some importers continue to complain that this may mean that they could retroactively face a significant increase in tariffs after they have, in good faith, imported goods, paid the tariff that was in force at that time, and then sold those goods at a price which was based on the tariff that was in force at that time.
The purpose of this is simply to ensure that if a tariff is retroactively increased, then an importer who brought in goods in good faith is not unreasonably penalized.
I understand that the Government has established an interdepartmental review board with respect to tariffs that may need to be reviewed under Clause 139. The Government will probably argue that this is sufficient. However, our argument still is that where retroactive action increases a tariff, it would be unreasonable to penalize importers who had acted in good faith. The Government's response is useful but does not obviate the need for our amendment.

adversely affect smaller businesses or people who operate quite clearly in good faith.
One can think of many examples of how companies would not have the ability to recover those costs. For example, a company that imports a widget with a 10 per cent tariff would add that cost to the retailer who, in turn, would add his markup when selling it to the consumer. If the Government informs the company a year and a half later that it has increased the tariff to 25 per cent, the only source of that increased cost will be the operating capital of the company. Such a situation could put companies at risk.
I am certain the interdepartmental committee would take that into consideration, but I would rather see an error made on the side of caution in this matter and provide protection by eliminating the retroactivity.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join my colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), in support of this amendment. The decisions of the Government in regard to tariffs and the prospect of future changes to tariffs are so uncertain that my constituents have difficulty in taking orders for imported products which they sell. They have difficulty putting in orders because they do not know what rate of tariff they will have to pay, if any tariff at all. Since they are unable to quote a price to a prospective customer, they are in no position to make an order in the country from which they hope to import the product.
Let me deal for a few moments with some comments made earlier today by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He talked very proudly about the fact that substantially more people have found jobs since the Government took office, and that the rate of unemployment is at its lowest in a number of years.
While that is true, it is reported in the Ottawa Citizen today that Ottawa, one of the most prosperous cities in the country, expects an increase of 9 per cent in the welfare rolls in the coming year. The same report has come from Toronto, probably the most prosperous city with one of the lowest rates of unemployment in the country, as well as from my City of Winnipeg.
Let us keep in mind what that means. According to the National Council on Welfare, in every city and province in this country, people on welfare are living substantially below the poverty line. In fact, it has been estimated that in 1986 people receiving social assistance lived from 20 per cent to 53 per cent below the generally accepted poverty line. In some cities such as Toronto, 70 per cent of the benefits they receive goes for payment of rent. That is not supposed to be the case, but the fact is that the price of rental accommodation in major cities such as Ottawa, Toronto, and Vancouver is substantially higher than the rent calculation in the monthly welfare cheque made by the provinces.
The Minister also boasted about, as he calls it, his plan to reform the tax system. I remind the Minister that the parliamentary committee that looked at his White Paper, a committee of nine members, seven of whom were fellow Conservatives, said that the federal Government's changes to the standard tax deduction for dependant children will slash benefits from middle income families and do nothing for the poor taxpayers. The proposed changes, coupled with other measures introduced by the Conservative Government since 1984, will cut real child benefits by half or more for upper and middle-income families by 1991. In other words, the people who will really gain from the Minister's proposed tax changes will be precisely those who-I see a Member opposite shaking his head, indicating that what I am saying is not correct. Let me put on the record some of the facts with respect to income distribution and who gets what. In 1981, the top 20 per cent of income earners enjoyed 45 per cent of the national income. The bottom 20 per cent enjoyed just 4 per cent of the national income. If we look at the wealthy, it is even worse. The top 20 per cent income earners enjoyed 68 per cent of the national wealth, while the bottom 20 per cent owned less than 1 per cent of the national wealth. Indeed, it is even worse than that because the top 10 per cent of income earners owned more than 50 per cent of the wealth.
Among the 20 western industrialized countries, Canada has the lowest over-all tax on wealth. Canada is the only industrialized country that permits large amounts of wealth to be accumulated and to be passed between generations without tax liability. I remind the Member who disagrees with me that it was the present Minister of Finance who proposed a year or so ago that there be no tax on the first $500,000 of capital gains.
Canada does not have an annual net wealth tax as do countries such as Germany, Austria, Norway, Sweden, Belgium and Denmark. In 1985, one in six Canadians lived in poverty. In 1986, the top 1 per cent of high-income Canadians, 63,000 families, had average incomes of $212,000 a year. I also remind the Member that 258 Canadians with incomes over $100,000 paid no income tax at all.
Let us look at corporations and the way the corporation tax system operates. I remind Members that the last major tax change to benefit the wealthy, introduced by the then Liberal Government-
